newsitem.title: USA: BA/AA merger could raise fares - U.S. consumer study.
newsitem.headline: BA/AA merger could raise fares - U.S. consumer study.

text.p: An alliance between American Airlines, a unit of AMR Corp., and British Airways Plc. could raise U.S.-U.K. fares substantially unless many more landing slots were opened at London's Heathrow airport, a study released Tuesday said.

The Consumer Federation of America study said the alliance, proposed last year by the two airlines, could cost travelers more than $500 million a year in higher fares, raising the cost of tickets by 20 to 40 percent.
The study called for American and BA to divest themselves of 560-840 slots a week at London Heathrow airport, about 25 percent of their holdings, to open the popular airport to competing airlines.

The U.S. Transportation Department has said it would not approve the alliance, and the necessary antitrust immunity, unless Washington and London first signed a free market air agreement, including opening new Heathrow slots to other U.S. carriers.

"Open skies" talks resumed in Washington on Tuesday. They have been held off and on over the past two years, with U.S. demands that Britain cede Heathrow slots to other carriers a major stumbling block.
American and BA have argued that their link would increase competition because the "open skies" accord that would precede it would allow many additional U.S. flights to Heathrow.

Mark Cooper, the federation's research director, said that if only a few slots were relinquished, they could end up with only a few American carriers who could then create "fortress airports" in the United States which they would dominate.
He said Northwest Airlines Corp. could dominate Detroit for flights to Heathrow, as would Delta Air Lines Inc. dominate Atlanta and USAir Group Philadelphia.
"We would like the Administration to take a hard look at this market," Cooper said and called for public hearings.
"Where competition exists," he said, "consumers get good prices. Where it doesn't, they don't."
